identificationRemarks: After looking at this again, I'm pretty sure now it is vittata. At 15cm, it is not a juvenile. Note the white dorsal fin tips, small scales without contrasting borders, dark mark above the iris, red band on gill cover that wouldn't show if the body color was not pale. Remember, nearly all fish can pale or intensify their colors at will. You have to work with that markings are visible. I first thought kuntee because if you assume the bar on the gill cover will also darken when the body color darkens, then that seems a better match. But those white dorsal spine tips...

I recently looked into the Eviota melasma vs E. pictifacies issue and concluded, apparently like you, that the stated visual differentiating features are subtle and tricky to apply. The main ones are more prominent and distinct red spots on cheeks and light/dark marks on the iris in E. pictifacies compared to E. melasma. In that sense my image corresponds to the E. pictifacies image in the description of that paper (Fig. 5). On that basis I updated the ID for this image to E. pictifacies. The main morphological difference stated in that paper is that the pelvic-fin rays are shorter and stouter in E. pictifacies, and are connected by membranes vs. not connected in E. melasma. But later in that same section they comment that "*Only E. melasma from Australia, the type locality, has the distinctive slender pelvic-fin rays not joined by membranes and a dark scleral area. Other similar species, and those called E. melasma from other areas, have stouter rays that are joined by membranes and varying eye colors*." That makes me wonder if the true E. melasma shouldn't be restricted to the Australian population and in my private image collection I have renamed all my E. melasma to E. pictifacies. There is variantion between them, including the reddish marking behind the eye, but until further research finds evidence of this being a species complex I think using E. pictifacies is appropriate. In addition, I do not know if and how iNaturalist allows adding "cf." in species names as it would often come in handy.
